Sacred origins

Where did it all begin?

Each tradition tells its own story of beginnings, and none is forced into another’s frame. Sacred accounts are labelled as such; the scientific model is labelled separately. Select up to three to read side by side.

Many believers hold their tradition’s account alongside the scientific model, reading it literally, symbolically or theologically. Views differ within every tradition. Summaries here are brief introductions; follow the listed sources for the texts themselves.

Compare beliefs

Choose two to five traditions to see where they agree, where they partly agree and where they differ. Each is described in its own terms.

How do we reach paradise?

How each tradition describes reaching the ultimate good. These are conceptual pathways, not formulas: every tradition teaches that its steps are lived together, and each has schools that describe them differently.

Marriage and family

How scripture, later tradition and modern law describe marriage across traditions — clearly separating what a text reports from what a tradition teaches today.

Evidence gaps

How long after a life or a teaching were things first written down, and how old are the oldest copies we still have? The same yardstick is used for every tradition.

Lifetime (dashed if traditional or uncertain)Earliest outside mentionWritten downOldest surviving copy

A gap is not a judgement. Many traditions preserved teachings by careful memorisation, and later manuscripts can faithfully copy much older texts. Dates follow mainstream scholarship; traditional dates are marked.

Guided tours

Short journeys through the timeline. The camera moves from stop to stop with a caption; press Pause at any time, or Details to read more.

Alphabets: one family of scripts

Hebrew, Arabic, Greek and Latin letters all descend from the alphabet first used around Sinai and spread by the Phoenicians. Each row follows one letter.

The first column shows the Egyptian hieroglyphs that early alphabet signs are thought to be modelled on. Hebrew square script and Arabic descend via Aramaic (Arabic via Nabataean). Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, ‘Alphabet’; Healey, The Early Alphabet (1990).

Sacred calendars

Why do some festivals move? The Islamic calendar is purely lunar — about 354 days — so Ramadan starts about 11 days earlier each solar year and circles the seasons in about 33 years. Easter follows both moon and sun, so it stays in spring. Nowruz is fixed to the March equinox.

2026

Ramadan dates are calculated with the tabular Islamic calendar; actual dates depend on moon sighting and may differ by one or two days. Easter is the Western (Gregorian) date.
